abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.

sections.body: Agent outcomes depend on both the model and the harness, which controls context, tools, and lifecycle. Existing benchmarks score mainly final results, which give limited insight into whether harness mechanisms function. The paper introduces TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components and uses 95 mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth. Trajectory tracing, multi-source evidence, and failure attribution modules support a two-layer evaluation. The authors evaluate 3,420 selected executions across four harnesses and nine models.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Outcome-only benchmarks give limited insight into harness mechanisms, so the paper proposes separate harness evaluation.

sections.body: The paper defines an agent as a model plus a harness, where the harness builds context, exposes tools, transports results, keeps state, and enforces permissions. Harness reliability concerns faithful information delivery and execution, and it does not guarantee task success, since a model can decide wrongly after receiving accurate information. The benchmark therefore assigns separate criteria to agent outcomes and harness obligations. The paper also separates four levels of claim: a criterion verdict, a confirmed harness defect, an activated candidate link, and a validated propagation. Apparatus failure is treated as a measurement limitation, not a harness defect.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: An agent is a model plus a harness, and harness reliability is judged separately from whether the task succeeds.

sections.body: The benchmark asks whether the agent produced required artifacts and actions, whether the native harness preserved needed information and execution behavior, and whether an agent failure matches a predeclared propagation mechanism. Runs pass an apparatus admission gate covering container lifecycle, archive integrity, and trace scoreability before semantic scoring. Trajectories are reconstructed in a shared intermediate representation with provenance preserved. Evidence is selected deterministically for each criterion. Candidate links are activated automatically when the linked harness and agent criteria both fail and activation conditions hold. The authors state that confirming a harness defect or propagation requires validation beyond automated scoring.
sections.heading: TraceTrial-Bench
sections.headline: The benchmark scores agent and harness layers separately, then links failed harness criteria to agent failures via predeclared mechanism chains.

sections.body: Four native harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek Harness, and OpenClaw) run nine model configurations over the same 95 tasks, producing 855 cells per harness and 380 per model. Each cell contains one selected execution with a final archived evaluation. The data contains no independent repetitions, so within-cell repeatability is not estimated. Runs execute in Docker with the task workspace mounted at `/workspace`, and wall-time limits span 120–5,400 seconds. All 3,420 final evaluations use `deepseek-v4-flash` as a separate semantic judge, though per-criterion output limits vary. Durations are not interpreted as a controlled throughput comparison.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Four harnesses, nine models, and 95 tasks form a full matrix of 3,420 cells, each with one selected execution.

sections.body: Across all 3,420 cells, 14,979 of 20,016 Agent items pass (74.8%) and 19,242 of 28,188 Harness items pass (68.3%). A total of 1,351 runs (39.5%) satisfy every Agent criterion, but only 286 (8.4%) satisfy every criterion in both layers. Claude Code has the highest Agent pass rate at 44.0% and the highest overall score at 73.5. OpenClaw has the highest Harness macro rate at 72.0% and the highest clean rate at 11.7%. Codex is lowest on Harness macro at 59.8%.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Claude Code leads task success at 44.0% while OpenClaw leads harness macro at 72.0%, so the two rankings differ.
